transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-04
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Martin (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Redwood Solutions), Maria Gomez (BrightSearch Head of Search), Raj Patel (BrightSearch ML Eng), Derek Liu (BrightSearch Infra), Ellen Cho (Product)

Summary (auto): deep dive on embeddings + reranking performance and unit cost tradeoffs. Discussed vector dimensions (128/256/512), batching strategies, KV cache hit modeling, quantized model profiles (INT8/4-bit), VPC/on-prem constraints, and target latency SLOs (P95 75ms for online rerank; offline batch throughput for embedding generation). Next steps: share benchmarks, pilot scoping, send security docs.

00:00:03 Sophie: okay everyone thanks for jumping on, we've got about an hour, want to cover the microbenchmarks we ran and then pair on what you want to measure for your reranker and embed pipeline
00:00:12 Maria: thanks Sophie, yes main thing for us is we need to get down to at least P95 75ms on our 2-stage search rerank otherwise the UX suffers, right now we're at ~150 P95 with their current stack
00:00:29 Liam: got it, and just so I'm clear, is that 75ms end-to-end for the client call or just the reranker stage?
00:00:35 Maria: the reranker stage — the local first-pass is ~40ms but the neural rerank must fit under 75ms ideally
00:00:43 Raj: quick context — current infra is a mix of hosted embeddings service and an on-prem rerank model behind our VPC, we also do nightly bulk embedding refreshes for ranking updates
00:01:05 Sophie: good detail. quick outline: we'll go over batch size and vector dims tradeoffs, KV cache behavior for repeated prefixes, quantization impact on latency and topk quality, then discuss deployment modes — hosted vs dedicated vs private, and what Derek needs for VPC/on-prem
00:01:25 Derek: for us network is the usual gotcha — we need to ensure TLS peer and no egress to public endpoints, so Private with customer-managed control plane is attractive if latency is tight
00:01:40 Jordan: also want to flag cost constraints — they care about per-1M request token-equivalents and embedding unit cost for nightly recomputes
00:01:55 Liam: great. starting with vector dims: our internal benchmarks (toy-repro) show that going from 512->256 dims reduces latency ~18% at same batch size, and 256->128 gives another ~22% improvement but with diminishing rerank quality depending on model and quantization. we typically test dims [128,256,512] for semantic similarity usecases
00:02:24 Raj: hmm quality is the main concern. for reranking top-10 we measure MRR and nDCG, we've seen 256 capture most signal but need to test on your quantized stacks
00:02:40 Liam: exactly. we recommend running your top-100 queries through 3 profiles: full float fp16 512, fp16 256, and INT8/quant 256; that gives a tradeoff curve. we can run those on Dedicated/GPU to get P95 numbers
00:03:02 Sophie: I'll note that our "Optimize" suggestions will recommend the lowest dim that stays within your eval threshold — we'll automate per-candidate metrics in the benchmark sheet
00:03:18 Maria: ok, and for batch sizes, what range should we expect for low latency? our traffic is bursty, many small interactive queries but also some larger batch jobs
00:03:33 Liam: for interactive rerank we usually keep micro-batches (1-8) for single-request latency; continuous batching helps but adds queuing. example: on a V100-class GPU, batch=1 for 512-dim quantized model yields ~35-45ms per call; batch=4 improves throughput but P95 increases due to queueing if arrival rate is low. You want to tune a latency SLO-driven batcher
00:04:02 Derek: can you quantify queueing effect? if we set batch window to 20ms, what's typical P95 increase?
00:04:10 Liam: depends on QPS. at 50 QPS, a 20ms window doesn't add much; at 5 QPS you'll often wait full window and see P95 add ~15-25ms. Our Smart batching module adjusts window dynamically by traffic shape
00:04:28 Raj: what about KV cache — we have a lot of repeated prefixes for chat-style rerank contexts, can caching help a lot?
00:04:37 Liam: yes, KV cache for autoregressive models helps a ton for multi-turn generation. For embeddings/rerank it's different: if your reranker uses cached dense vectors for candidates, that avoids recomputing embeddings for static docs. we also support prefix-level KV cache for decoder models to speed generation. In practice, caching candidate embeddings reduces per-request work especially for cold-start and long document sets
00:05:05 Maria: so for our case, where we rerank top-100 scored candidates that rarely change, we should serve precomputed embeddings and only recompute when fresher signals arrive?
00:05:14 Liam: yep. maintain a candidate vector store (we integrate with vector DBs or can host in Dedicated memory). for top-100 it's cheap to load vectors from RAM—latency is low. main cost is I/O if store is on remote disk or networked DBs
00:05:31 Derek: how does that look in Private mode — do we host vector store in customer VPC? any special network patterns?
00:05:39 Sophie: Private deployment can colocate the runtime and vector store inside your VPC. we support peered subnets and direct peering; traffic stays internal. Derek, you'll want to validate that your firewall allows the runtime to reach your vector store ports and the KMS endpoints for key access
00:05:56 Derek: noted. on quantization: how safe is INT8 for reranking quality? we saw mixed results with 4-bit on some models
00:06:05 Liam: INT8 is generally safe for many open models on rerank tasks, but model-dependent. 4-bit (QLoRA/4-bit) can be very cost-efficient but has higher variance; we run profile evals to show expected delta in MRR/nDCG. our quantized kernels are optimized to use fused kernels for attention so latency gains are real — often 1.5-2x speedup relative to fp16 on the same GPU for decode-heavy workloads
00:06:36 Raj: does KV cache work with those quantized kernels? any compatibility gotchas?
00:06:42 Liam: yes, KV cache is supported; the cache stores key/value tensors in a dequantized internal format for stable ops. there is a small mem/compute tradeoff but it's worth it for multi-step generation. for reranking that doesn't autoregenerate we usually bypass KV cache and rely on precomputed embeddings
00:06:58 Ellen: a practical question — for our nightly embedding refreshes of ~5M documents, what's a recommended approach to avoid cost spikes?
00:07:07 Liam: run bulk embedding generation on Dedicated reserved capacity during off-peak, use model parallelism and large batches (256-1024) to maximize throughput. also use sharded batching and async workers to hide latency. quantized FP16/INT8 can reduce GPU hours significantly for large jobs
00:07:29 Sophie: and Redwood Optimize can recommend batching profiles — we'll include a suggested schedule in the benchmark sheet to smooth compute usage
00:07:40 Maria: on the subject of metrics, we care about P50/P95/P99 and tail jitter — do you have tracing hooks?
00:07:47 Liam: yes we expose per-request token-level traces, per-route histograms, and exporting to OpenTelemetry. you'll get latency breakdown (model runtime, queue time, network, KV cache hits)
00:08:02 Derek: security: if we do Private, how is key management handled? we need KMS/HSM and audit logs
00:08:09 Sophie: we support customer-managed KMS in Private (bring-your-own KMS) and HSM integrations are available. audit logs for inference calls and model pulls are captured and can be forwarded to your SIEM
00:08:19 Maria: good. can you send the SOC2 & ISO summaries again?
00:08:24 Sophie: yes I'll attach them after the call
00:08:30 Liam: moving to concrete numbers — we ran a few microbenchmarks on a 80GB A100 and a 48GB A40. here are representative numbers (these are approximate and will vary by model):
00:08:42 Liam: sample profile 1: fp16, 512-dim rerank encoder, batch=1, no KV cache, p95 ~48ms on A100; batch=4 p95 ~70ms but throughput increases 3x
00:08:55 Liam: profile 2: int8-quant 256-dim, batch=1 p95 ~30ms on A100; batch=4 p95 ~45ms; throughput 2.5-3x vs fp16 512
00:09:10 Liam: profile 3 (large batch bulk embed): fp16 512, batch=512, amortized embed throughput ~60k docs/hour per GPU depending on token lengths
00:09:24 Raj: those numbers are helpful. do you have variance with sequence length? our queries are short, mostly <64 tokens for rerank context but candidates are 256 tokens average
00:09:37 Liam: sequence length on the candidate side affects encode time; candidate embedding cost scales with tokens. for encoder-only rerankers it's linear-ish in tokens x dims. our benchmarks above assume candidates avg 256 tokens. shorter contexts will improve latency proportionally
00:09:55 Maria: what's the expected per-1M request cost range if we use Dedicated versus hosted? just ballpark for comparison
00:10:04 Sophie: ballpark — hosted API with mixed models is often higher per-call but simpler; Dedicated amortizes GPU hours. example rough: hosted inline rerank at p95 targets might cost $X per 1M calls (we'll put exact in sheet) while Dedicated fixed cost + run-time yields lower unit cost at scale but requires commit. we'll include a model to show break-even points at your volume
00:10:23 Jordan: can you remind us about fallbacks — if Dedicated is saturated do you route to hosted?
00:10:30 Liam: yes you can set routing policies: priority is Dedicated, then Hosted warm pool or smaller model variants. automatic fallback to a cheaper model or region keeps availability up; quality drop is reported in traces so you can monitor regressions
00:10:46 Derek: on telemetry: do you provide per-request IDs we can attach to prod logs for correlation?
00:10:51 Liam: yes, request IDs and trace IDs; we also include token-level summaries and model variant metadata in traces
00:11:00 Maria: let's talk about evaluation — you mentioned we'll get MRR deltas for quantization. how do you compute that?
00:11:07 Liam: we run your eval set through the baseline float model and the quantized variants and compute MRR/nDCG and provide per-query deltas; we also surface examples where quantization changes ranking order so you can review
00:11:22 Raj: is there a quick threshold you recommend? like <1% MRR drop acceptable?
00:11:27 Liam: many teams accept <0.5-1% relative drop for large cost savings, but it depends on product sensitivity. we'll make this configurable in the benchmark
00:11:35 Maria: for our product, even 0.5% MRR is noticeable on engagement, so we'd prefer to target under 0.2% if possible
00:11:44 Sophie: noted — we'll prioritize running the highest-fidelity quant profiles to get tight estimates
00:11:50 Liam: another point — vector dimension reduction sometimes helps more than quantization for latency without hurting recall if you retrain a small linear projection head. that's worth an experiment: 512->256 with fp16 can match baseline for some tasks
00:12:08 Raj: good call, we have a small budget for a retrain/PRoject like that
00:12:14 Maria: operationally, we want to maintain fresh embeddings — can Redwood help with incremental embedding recompute?
00:12:21 Liam: yes, we support incremental syncs: recompute vectors for changed docs via event-driven jobs; avoid full re-index when only a slice changes. we can wire to your data pipeline to trigger jobs on updates
00:12:34 Derek: network again — if we run Private, will workload spikes saturate our NICs? what's recommended NIC sizing for 3 A100s?
00:12:42 Liam: depends on throughput; for dense vector loads with 256 dims, plan for 25-50 Gbps per GPU at high QPS. we usually recommend 100GbE for multi-GPU nodes to avoid network bottlenecks if you're centralizing vector stores separately
00:12:58 Maria: let's pivot to concrete pilot plan — what would a 4-week pilot look like?
00:13:05 Sophie: typical pilot: week 1: log/sample collection and benchmark plan; week 2: run microbenchmarks on your eval set with dims/quant profiles; week 3: integrate Dedicated or Private runtime with a small traffic % for A/B; week 4: analyze results, cost model, and recommend production roll-out. deliverables: benchmark sheet, quality deltas, and infra runbook
00:13:27 Raj: do we need to give you our production data or a sample is fine?
00:13:31 Liam: a representative sample (top-100 queries + distribution) is enough to estimate, but full logs help for traffic modeling. we'll accept anonymized samples
00:13:42 Sophie: quick Q for Derek — for Private deployment, do you want a fully air-gapped on-prem or VPC-hosted Private with peering?
00:13:50 Derek: VPC-hosted is preferred; fully air-gapped is harder for our org due to ops overhead
00:13:56 Sophie: great, that aligns with what we've done for other customers. we'll produce a network runbook and sample Security Group rules
00:14:05 Maria: any other limitations or gotchas we should be aware of?
00:14:10 Liam: two small ones: 1) quantization can change calibration of embeddings so thresholds for downstream heuristics might shift; 2) model variants must be pinned across releases to avoid drift — we'll suggest model pinning with rollouts
00:14:26 Raj: about model pinning — can we do canary rollouts for a subset of queries?
00:14:31 Liam: yes, Redwood Console supports canary and A/B traffic splits, and automatic rollback if quality regressions exceed thresholds
00:14:38 Ellen: how do you surface quality regressions? email? console alerts? webhooks?
00:14:43 Sophie: console alerts + webhooks for your monitoring + email summaries. we'll also create eval sets that trigger if MRR drops past X%
00:14:55 Maria: okay great. can you walk us through an example microbenchmark you'll run for us?
00:15:00 Liam: sure. step 1: ingest your top-100 eval queries and the candidate sets. step 2: run three model profiles: fp16-512 baseline, fp16-256, int8-256. For each profile we run batch sizes [1,2,4,8] and measure P50/P95/P99, throughput, and memory usage. step 3: simulate traffic patterns from your logs to measure queueing effects. step 4: capture quality metrics MRR/nDCG. step 5: produce a sheet with tradeoff curves and recommended config per SLO
00:15:34 Raj: how long does that take to run?
00:15:36 Liam: for a ~10k eval set it's typically 2-4 hours on a small Dedicated cluster; for larger evals maybe overnight
00:15:43 Maria: what about embedding dimensionality experiments — how are those measured?
00:15:49 Liam: run the same eval with projected vectors 512/256/128 and compare recall and rerank quality. if you have a fine-tuned head we can include that in the evaluation
00:15:58 Derek: curious on hardware — assumed A100 numbers; if we run on cheaper GPUs like T4 or A40 how much slower?
00:16:06 Liam: T4 is OK for embeddings but less ideal for large-scale rerank; P95s increase and throughput drops. A40 performs closer to A100 for inference depending on kernel availability; we'll include comparative numbers in the benchmark
00:16:18 Jordan: competitor question — we use Pinecone for vector store now; how would integration look?
00:16:24 Sophie: we integrate with Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, and can also host an in-memory store if you prefer. integration is via SDK or HTTP and we can instrument retrieval latencies in our traces
00:16:36 Maria: any final questions?
00:16:40 Derek: one more on billing for Dedicated — how granular are usage charges? per-GPU-hour?
00:16:46 Sophie: Dedicated is typically a reserved monthly commit plus overage per GPU-hour for burst; we'll provide the pricing template in the follow-up
00:16:55 Liam: last technical note: for rerank we sometimes convert the reranker to a bi-encoder for fast approximate nearest neighbor retrieval then run a small cross-encoder on top of top-K; that hybrid reduces compute while keeping quality high. it's a good architecture if you have a large candidate corpus
00:17:15 Raj: that might fit our scale — good idea
00:17:19 Maria: okay thanks — let's recap next steps
00:17:23 Sophie: recap: 1) Redwood to run microbenchmarks (Liam) and share sheet, 2) Customer to send sample logs and evaluation set (Raj), 3) Derek to validate VPC/network constraints, 4) Sophie to send security docs and draft pricing. we'll target initial benchmark results by 2025-11-10
00:17:41 Ellen: sounds good to me
00:17:44 Maria: thanks everyone, we'll sync after the benchmark
00:17:47 Sophie: great thanks, wrapping up now

(Transcript continues with brief wrap and signoffs; remaining time included Q&A on small ops details and confirming dates)

End of transcript.
